thread.title: Will Apple’s New HomePod Soon Dominate Hi-fi Profits?

author: Nathaniel Wice
title: Will Apple’s New HomePod Soon Dominate Hi-fi Profits?
text:
Apple's $349 HomePod smart speaker delivers great sound, better than competitors such as Amazon's Echo line of appliances. Voice control is good, though could be better. Pricey , with aggravating voice control, and a shortsighted lock-in to Apple ’s ( AAPL ) second-banana streaming music subscription, Apple Music .
Those are among the gripes contained in the mixed reviews of HomePod , Apple's $349 voice-enabled speaker system , that is the company's answer to Amazon ( AMZN ) " Echo " line of smart speakers. Amazon has sold millions of Echo units, since they first caught on three years ago, and beating the Echo is no mean feat.
Our hunch though, having lived with the HomePod since its release last Friday, is that, as some have suggested , Apple may soon dominate hi-fi speaker profits, just as it was recently estimated that the three-year-old Apple Watch outgrossed the entire Swiss watch industry over the holidays, Rolex, Omega, and Swatch combined.
Wall Street likes it
For sure, Wall Street likes the subscription story , with double-digit growth in service revenue to sooth fears of saturated iPhone markets. Apple Music is still only about half of Spotify’s 70 million paid subscribers worldwide, but it’s set to surpass Spotify in the U.S., as reported last week in The Wall Street Journal , and widely represents a successful transition for Apple not only from song sales to streaming, but also a growing talent for exclusive content in the age of Netflix.
As Morgan Stanley ’s Katy Huberty praised Apple’s most recent earnings: “Services is…contributing over 30% of gross profit by the end of 2021 … allowing for…EPS growth even without device revenue growth.”
Maybe this is why HomePod at launch only streams natively from Apple Music , a common complaint of early reviewers. Spotify and other music sources can actually play through HomePod from an iPhone, iPad, using Apple’s wireless Airplay protocol, but even on the iPhone there are no Siri voice commands to control third-party music services and podcast players. (You must have an iOS device, you cannot use a Mac to set it up.)
These complaints will redouble if Apple’s developer conference in June comes and goes without Spotify controls in Siri. The hi-fi market itself has been upended by Amazon’s voice-controlled Echo, a surprise hit that first took off in in 2015.
Echo has forced speaker makers, such as Sonos , which was already one of the best on the market at the time , and Bose , to add Alexa controls It turns out people really like being able to casually say, play Fela Kuti or the Rolling Stones or “Hotel California.”
Great sound, great integration
Play your first song on the dense little HomePod—it’s only 6.8 inches tall, and setup is simple so long as you are already an iOS user—and it will quickly size up the room, using its microphone array and built-in iOS brain to bounce sound off walls and fill the room with a big 3D sound.
Multiple HomePods will be able to work together with a software update this year, Apple promises. No such promises for native Spotify support, which would clearly help HomePod sales.
Consumer Reports said meh , but other audio engineer experts have gushed , including the co-founder of competitor Sonos.
HomePod sounds better to us than a good bookshelf speaker, and miles ahead of the now $85 Echo that won over our music listening with voice-control convenience ("Alexa, play Fela Kuti," "Alexa, Is it going to rain today?" "Alexa, what's the population of Thailand?" "Alexa, turn off the lights").
HomePod's own voice control is merely okay—and will presumably continue to improve—but the HomePod sound-engineering software works magic to minimize bass distortion even at high volume. This eliminates the usual clipping we're used to in, say, a car stereo when played loud. HomePod made us wish we still threw dorm parties.
The HomePod also works seamlessly with Apple’s smart home system, and doubles as a better speakerphone than we have at the office.
Audiofiles gonna hate
Some of this software intervention in the sound of songs will drive high-end sound people bonkers, along with the absence of any line-in for digital or analog audio, and there will always be audiophiles like our friends at Bridgehampton ’s Sunrise Smarthome , who swear by lossless, high-bitrate music collections managed with Roon software , and played through a $4,800 digital-to-analog converter , and a $2,400 tube amp , hardwired to $6,000 speakers .
Where are those Apple shows?
Now, if only Siri knew about its own Apple Music shows . That broad deficiency, still present this week, is amazing to behold, in our experience, hiding great, exclusive weekly programs by the likes of Elton John and A Tribe Called Quest's Q-Tip. They have been hidden from voice control with Siri for years now (although the shows can be found through Beats1 links in iTunes and the Apple Music app). It's as if the restaurant chef had laid in fine cuts of filet mignon advertised on the daily specials but the waiters and waitresses had no way to take the order. "Hey, Siri, play Mike D's show on Beats1 Radio." "Sorry, I couldn't find Mike D's show on Beats1 Radio."
